Went through and verified heater operations.
Found that this vehicle has the heater circuit wired differently than our new standards.
Blower motor and heater contactor are trigged by the same switch using the same output from the PDU.
At this point in time upper management says that this should be fine since our older cars have been wired this way without any major issues.
The proper fix to this would be to move the contactor positive lead over to the "AC Blower" positive in the HVAC sub and have it commanded on based on the current level of the Heat Blower output from the pmu. This prevents the heater from turning on unless there is a load present on the heater blower motor.
However as the vehicle sits the heater is enabled and works as built.
Also Uploaded the current PMU Project files to the drive under the vehicle folder. That way this can be referenced in the future if necessary.If any PMU changes are made we will need to reupload or replace what was there.

comments.author: Brandon Beaman
comments.text:
Progress Report — Parking Brake EStopp Actuator Current Analysis
Date: 9/9/2026 System: VCM_517 — Parking Brake / EStopp Pawl Actuator Logged by: Brandon Beaman
Summary
Reviewed five Raptor-Cal test logs of the parking brake pawl actuator (PrkPwlO15) to characterize peak current draw against actuator timing calibration and identify any correlation worth flagging for calibration tuning.
Work Performed
Pulled and parsed five sequential VCM_517 Parking Brake logs (11:47:16, 11:51:09, 11:54:52, 12:00:45, 12:08:36) for the measured actuator current channel (PrkPwlO15_P27_Measured_Current) and the EStopp actuator timing calibration fields (PrkActMnTime_EStopp, PrkActMxTime_EStopp, PrkActReleaseTime_EStopp).
Extracted peak current draw and its timestamp from each log.
Cross-referenced peak draw against each log's actuation timing setpoints to check for a relationship between calibration and real-world current pull.
Compiled a comparison table and written analysis of findings (delivered as a standalone report, both Markdown and PDF).
Findings

undefined
Across Logs 1–4, shortening either the min or max actuation time window was associated with a higher peak current pull — a preliminary pattern worth further testing.
Log 5 breaks that pattern: it shares identical timing calibration with Log 4 (Min 4.250 s / Max 6.000 s / Release 3.500 s) but produced the highest peak draw of the whole set (12.25 A vs. Log 4's 10.25 A) — a 2 A swing with no calibration change. This points to run-to-run mechanical/electrical variability rather than a purely timing-driven effect, and suggests more repeat runs at fixed timing are needed before drawing conclusions.
Release Time was held constant (3.500 s) across all five tests and was not a variable in this data set.
Next Steps / Open Items
Run repeat tests at fixed timing calibration (e.g., hold Log 4/5's settings) to quantify normal run-to-run variance in peak draw before attributing changes to calibration.
Once variance is characterized, revisit the min/max actuation time trend with a larger sample to confirm or rule it out.

Side Note:
It looks / feels like its more dependent on how much pedal pressure is being applied when the vehicle is commanded to go into park. If you have just enough pedal in it to prevent the vehicle from rolling the Amp draw is higher. If you're heavy in the pedal then the amp draw is lower.
This might make the current based engagement unreliable. Set it low enough to not throw a flag based on pedal pressure then you may end up with a light engagement.
Place it high enough to reach the max amp draw you may get a GML because the end user was holding the brake pedal harder when going into park.

comments.author: Brandon Beaman
comments.text:
Further testing shows that the slight rolling on an extreme road grade.
The road that I was testing on is Foremost here near the shop. The Approx grade of this road is 11°.
The vehicle makes a good effort to hold itself after the parking brake is engaged however without fail every time it does slowly roll away regardless if the car is facing up the hill or down the hill.
Multiple tests and test runs were performed to verify this data.
A couple key take aways here are that the E-Stopp is functioning exactly as it should and or at least within manufacturers specifications. Regardless of parking brake adjustments we add it will still only pull 10A reliably. There is nothing in our system that is preventing the E-Stopp from using up to 25A its just not requesting anything more.
Marc opted to return all the settings back to where they were previously set. He had Claude go through all of the old logs and look for a difference in settings changes and there were no major setting changes from today.
So we left the settings where they were except release timing. we add 0.8seconds to the release timing to hopefully help with the brake dragging when coming out of park.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Worked with Brandon to develop a better PMU revision system. Cleaned up the master branch and backed up on google drive. Had Brandon pull this down and showed him how to flash to the PMU's along with a number of other vehicle startup details to follow along first. Moved on to the VCU, showed Brandon about the firmware builds and Raptor structures. Converted vehicle requirements into a VCU config. Moved on to the inverter while Brandon loaded that. Upgraded the inverter firmware and flashed EEPROM in line with a W motor while following along in thee sheet.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Continued startup with Brandon and Dave. Hooked up HV and key'd on. Tried charging and got the ChgPortContFlt, verified all the associated wiring that has caused that fault previously, no problems found. Tried charging again and it just worked this time. Verified battery heater. Calibrated the resolver. Troubleshot cabin heater wiring. Searched and searched for documentation but couldn't find complete references. Experementially found the VCU was telling the PMU to tell the VCU to turn on the heat. Took thorough notes on actual wiring.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified K33 "Heat Request" functionality on Prehiem to make sure I had the correct tags in Raptor-Service. Tried various combinations of PMU outputs and VCU configs to determine if there was a way to get powering up the heater logic unit as the mechanism to enable heat. Ends up with a fault in the VCU which makes adding a relay the easier option. Drew a diagram for and wired up a relay to a spare output on the PMU. Wrote logic to check the temp knob below 15%, the fan knob above 30%, as well as negative contactor and ignition on. Tested all knob positions and GUI inputs while watching in Raptor and the PMU software. The GUI indicates correctly and warm air blows. I never let it heat up enough to judge effectiveness. Only thing left for HVAC now is to charge the AC and tune that in.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Verified heater circuit actually working by monitoring CAN data from the heater itself for output power. Double checked with a second data source Pack_Current from the BMS. Modified the PMU logic to also include fan and temp knobs as a criteria for turning on the cabin heat pump. Tested all scenarious with the user inputs from the GUI and knobs. Noticed the battery pump was running when it usually isn't, started to investigate, met for various discussions with the team before I could finish. Plugged into Preheim to investigate source of the difference in control.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Tuned in the AC compressor with Dave, it's working as expected plus a little 'bonus'. The AC compressor 'hiccups' with HV connected but the logic unit powered off. Powering up the compressor logic controller without Ampere commanding it to actually compress causes a VCU level fault. Shared to Slack.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Catching up on Slack before the meeting. Looked into Claudes diagnosis of the AC issue. Looks like the PMU program has never changed for that channel and Claude picked up on the troubleshooting I did as the actual problem, not knowing that at time the system was supposed to be operating different than the rest of the fleet. This was required to verify the 450V compressor functions differently than the 400V one and would work better under a different control sequence. Verified VCU settings for the battery were wrong and corrected.

comments.author: Devin DuMont
comments.text: Forced the car to suck out the BMS config again and the fully charged range estimate dropped from 306.04 to 149.58 miles. The new battery health calculations result in 146.4 Ah for the pack, a very reasonable estimate. Also verified Dave's findings on the AC compressor from the computer side. The hiccup issue has been magically fixed.
